Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version.

Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.

Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR.

My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles.

After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.

#7446. SDK Engineer - Python at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We're looking for a SDK Engineer - Python to join our SDK team and own how developers talk to Supabase from Python. You'll work closely with the rest of the SDK team, our Auth, Realtime, Storage, PostgREST, Functions, CLI and Docs teams, and the open-source community, helping us make the Python SDK a library Python developers genuinely enjoy using.

Python developers reach Supabase from backend services, data pipelines, notebooks, and a growing number of AI agents and agent frameworks. The Python SDK is how all of them talk to the platform: database queries, auth, storage, realtime and edge functions, in both sync and async flavors.

This is a library-authoring role, and the work happens in the open: public repos, public issue trackers, and API decisions whose consequences last for years. If you get satisfaction from a type checker that catches the bug before your users do, from an async client that cleans up after itself, and from an issue tracker that isn't a graveyard, you'll like it here.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and evolve our Python SDK across database, auth, storage, realtime and functions, with both sync and async APIs that feel natural in Python.

Start new things. Alongside the maintenance work, find what's missing, make the case for it, and build it. Nobody will hand you the list.

Work in the open. Triage inbound issues, review and shepherd outside contributions, keep CI and release automation healthy, and hold a clear, kind line on scope.

Own the typing experience. Make the SDK fully typed and checker-friendly, so autocomplete and static analysis stay correct in real codebases.

Keep us honest across environments. Multiple Python versions, sync and async frameworks, workers, serverless and notebooks — with dependency ranges that don't fight our users' projects. Test it, don't assume it.

Work on realtime. Long-lived websocket connections, reconnection, and subscription and presence semantics.

Track the platform. When auth, realtime, storage, postgrest or edge functions ship a change, make sure the SDK reflects it, and that we say so in the changelog.

Design in public. Write the RFCs, migration guides, release notes and docs. Treat a breaking change as a deprecation path plus a migration story, not a version bump.

Make our SDK legible to AI coding agents, which are now a major consumer of it.

Know modern Python typing deeply. You use generics, protocols, overloads and TypedDict as design tools, run strict type checking, and fix type errors without reaching for Any.

Have authored or maintained a published library with a public API and users outside your own company. You know what it costs to change something people depend on.

Know the maintainer side of open source. Issue triage at volume, reviewing outside PRs, release automation, changelogs and semver, security reports, and saying no to a feature request without losing the person who asked.

Are fluent in asyncio and have opinions on how a library should serve both sync and async callers.

Know Python packaging for libraries: pyproject.toml, wheels, modern tooling, version support policy, and why libraries shouldn't pin their dependencies tightly.

Test as a habit: unit, type-level and end-to-end against a real stack. Every fix comes with a regression test.

Write well. Design docs, changelogs and issue replies are a large part of the output here, much of it public, and we're async by default.

Have real autonomy: you find the important work, scope it, ship it, and say what you didn't do.

Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams

Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly

Bonus points if you: have run a major-version migration for a public package, know your way around JWT/OAuth, have built integrations for AI agent frameworks, or have generated idiomatic clients from a schema.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”

Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

New holiday data counts ads inside Google AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT across five shopping categories and shows which prompts ChatGPT ads ran on.

Adthena reported that approximately 175,100 paid ad placements were found within Google’s AI Overview panel as well as AI Mode panels inside the U.S. during the period of June to September. This included five holiday shopping categories; however, the majority of these paid placements belonged to apparel and consumer electronics.

The Holiday AI Paid Search Report also counts 204,489 ChatGPT ad placements in the same five categories over the same months. Adthena sells ad tracking for Google and ChatGPT, and the report closes with an offer for a free trial of its ChatGPT Ads product.

Some U.S. apparel and electronics advertisers may already be using portions of their existing campaigns to serve ads to users who see AI Overviews and AI Mode. The report identifies where the ads appeared, but does not track which ads were clicked, how much was spent, nor what conversions were achieved on either surface.

The total number of ads in Google’s AI Answers (in the U.S.) in this report is based upon a combined total for both AI Overviews and AI Mode. In that count, apparel has approximately 111,000 placements; consumer electronics have about 55,000; travel has roughly 6,500; beauty has about 2,100; and toys and games have around 685.

There are no separate ad buys for these placement types. According to Google’s Help Page regarding Ads in AI-Powered Experiences, all Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns that exist are automatically eligible to appear in AI-Answers. Although advertisers cannot specifically target only AI Overviews or AI Mode, or opt out of those placements apart from Search, they may still utilize negative keyword targeting and/or brand exclusions.

The report also reviewed how many times AI Overviews appeared in Google Results for both August of 2025 and August of 2026. Going from 304 million to 575 million, U.S. appearances saw an 89% increase over that period. The UK/EU saw an increase of 160%, while Australia saw an increase of 536%. The report doesn’t describe the queries behind those counts or say whether the set stayed the same across both years.

The report counts 204,489 ChatGPT Ads placements across five categories, Apparel, Consumer Electronics, Travel, Toys & Games and Beauty, from June through September 2026.

Adthena’s press release frames it more broadly, stating more than 200,000 advertisement placements occurred since OpenAI started allowing others to buy advertising space on the chatbot.

In the report’s count, apparel accounted for the largest number of advertisement placements at 90,517. Next was Consumer Electronics with 56,569; then Travel with 48,134; followed by Toys and Games with 4,694 and lastly Beauty with 4,575.

In addition, the company reported that there were 1,082 different advertisers in those five categories using the service in June, 3,741 advertisers in July, and 6,333 advertisers in August. The company projected the number of advertisers in September.

According to the report, the advertisers in its data in Toys and Games increased the most during that time frame from June to August, increasing 13 fold, from what the company calls a relatively low base.

The report states that the total number of advertiser placements included in their research covered all markets, but does not identify which markets or state whether they continued to monitor the same market(s)/queries throughout the entire four-month period. In addition, OpenAI expanded its footprint during that time.

On August 18, OpenAI announced that ChatGPT Ads would be available in 31 European countries. The company began offering this service one week later. Additionally, on September 23, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Ads to seven additional Asian markets.

For perspective, on October 21 OpenAI stated that more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT Ads since the advertising capability was opened up to outside parties just over eight months earlier. This figure represents all categories and the complete period of time that ChatGPT Ads has been open to third-party advertisers, so it isn’t directly comparable to the report’s monthly counts.

In addition to that, the report groups ChatGPT ads based on the nature of the search that an ad was run against. It describes research and discovery queries as “people comparing or asking what’s best rather than naming a product.”

In beauty, 83% of ads ran on those queries, while travel and toys & games were at 69% and 67% respectively. Apparel and consumer electronics came in under half, at 48% and 42% respectively.

Again, the press release references only the data related to beauty, travel and toys. The report provides no information about how questions were categorized.

Since Google includes searches that prompt ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode in aggregate in its standard reports for all of Search, they are intermingled throughout your search terms report.

In ChatGPT, best-of and comparison prompts carried most of the observed ads in beauty, travel & toys, and less than 50% of those seen in apparel and electronics.

After the report’s time frame closed, Google’s ads within their AI answers continued to evolve. Google announced that they were launching multi-turn ads in the United States on October 28. These allow advertisers’ ads to show up on subsequent searches (queries) in AI Mode. In addition, Google stated that ads in AI Mode are scaling to ten additional countries including Canada and Australia. They further stated that Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom were planned for Q4 2026.

OpenAI’s October 21 announcement expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries. The most recent Adthena data is from September so does not include these new developments nor the weeks surrounding Black Friday.

#7438. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7437. November Click Spikes In Google Search Console Are Bot Traffic – How To Filter Your Reports via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

That sudden click spike in Search Console isn’t real traffic. Here’s what my data shows, what’s causing it, and how to filter it out.

Earlier this week, I saw Barry Schwartz’s post on X (and his write-up on Search Engine Roundtable) sharing a screenshot from Joy Hawkins. Joy noticed that several sites were seeing sudden, massive vertical spikes in Google Search Console clicks while impressions stayed flat, and Barry asked a great follow-up question: “Anyone else seeing this? If so, how are you filtering the report…”

Screenshot of Barry Schwartz and Joy Hawkins’ post on X highlighting the sudden click spike in Google Search Console. (Image Credit: Marie Haynes)

When I saw Barry’s tweet, I immediately thought this would be the ultimate real-world test for Marie’s Brain – my soon-to-be-launched agentic SEO and AI search analysis system.

Over the past several months, I have been building Marie’s Brain to combine my 15+ years of research on Google’s ranking systems with live, programmatic access to the Search Console and analytics data of the sites I monitor. Instead of manually clicking through Search Console property by property to see if any of my clients were affected, I asked my system to scan across all of the sites I monitor, check the unfinalized fresh data through Nov. 2, 2026, and flag any property showing a sudden anomaly in clicks.

Within seconds, Marie’s Brain surfaced the exact same vertical spike across multiple sites in completely different industries – and pulled the raw page, query, device, and country dimensions so I could see what was actually happening under the hood.

Just like Glenn Gabe and Joy Hawkins mentioned in Barry’s Search Engine Roundtable post, the majority of properties I monitor showed completely normal traffic. However, while some SEOs saw the wave begin over the weekend (Oct. 31 to Nov. 1), a distinct subset of sites I monitor experienced a dramatic vertical spike on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 that mirrors Joy’s screenshot:

Six-month daily Google Search Console clicks (Search type: Web, including fresh unfinalized data through Nov. 2, 2026) across three affected properties I monitor. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Here is how those three anonymized properties behaved on Nov. 2, 2026 compared to their prior seven-day baseline (Oct. 26 – Nov. 1, 2026):

When I had my system drill into the raw API rows for Nov. 2, two unmistakable patterns emerged across the affected sites:

Visual summary of why total impressions look flat while automated deep-SERP clicks create a vertical spike in Google Search Console. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Normally, organic clicks in Search Console are heavily concentrated in the top 3 to 5 results on Page 1. On Nov. 2, click-through rate (CTR) exploded on pages ranking between Position 11 and Position 55 (Pages 2 through 6 of Google):

Why did total impressions stay flat if every click also had an impression? It comes down to simple scale. When a site normally gets 18,000 impressions and 50 clicks per day (like Site A), adding 275 automated impressions is only a 1.5% bump on the impression line – completely invisible on a chart! Adding 275 clicks to a 50-click baseline, on the other hand, creates a massive 6.5x vertical spike.

On Site C (a technical troubleshooting Q&A site), a single long-tail troubleshooting page that normally gets zero to one click per day (and never received more than seven clicks in a single day across the entire previous six months) suddenly jumped to 13 clicks on Nov. 1 and 40 clicks on Nov. 2.

While the spikes on Sites A and B came from U.S. searches, all 40 clicks on this Site C page came from Canada. From Oct. 28 to Oct.r 31, that page only had four to seven impressions per day in Canada (and 0 clicks) while ranking on Page 2. Then on Nov. 2, Canadian impressions on that page jumped by ~45 (to 50 impressions), and Canadian clicks jumped from 0 to 40 clicks – meaning almost every single one of those new impressions was clicked (an 80.0% CTR at average position 14.6 on Page 2, while U.S. clicks on that page stayed at 0)!

When I inspected the exact queries that clicked into that single URL on Nov. 2, there were 23 slightly reworded variations of the exact same troubleshooting question (including systematic number permutations like 3 times, 4 times, 5 times, 7 times, 10 times), almost every single one logging 100% CTR (1 click / 1 impression, 2/2, or 3/3) between Position 10.0 and Position 33.0. Other troubleshooting pages on the same site logged 1 click / 1 impression (100% CTR) at Position 45.5 to 54.0.

Normally, when a basic rank tracker or scraper loads a Google search results page, it only generates impressions – not clicks. For Search Console to record a click, a browser or bot has to actually follow (or trigger) Google’s click-tracking link on the search results page.

Looking at the data patterns across these sites, four possibilities stand out:

Because GSC does not let you filter the top performance chart by ranking position or CTR, there is no perfect one-click button to strip only the bot clicks out of your sitewide graph if dozens of pages were affected. However, these three approaches work well depending on how your site was impacted:

If dozens of pages across your whole site spiked on Desktop (like Sites A & B), you cannot exclude every page individually. While filtering the top bar by Device: Mobile obviously hides your legitimate Desktop traffic too, it is a great sanity check to show a client or stakeholder that your Mobile organic trendline is completely normal (on Site A, Mobile clicks were 30 on Nov 2 vs. 27-40 on prior days; on Site B, Mobile clicks were 11 on Nov 2 vs. 11 on Nov 1).

To see the exact pages that were affected on your site:

If you have Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, or an agentic coding environment (like Antigravity or Cursor) connected to the Google Search Console API or a custom MCP server, you can paste this exact prompt to check all of your sites in seconds:

No. Because this is automated activity rather than human visitors, you do not need to change your pages, disavow anything, or panic when those clicks drop right back down to baseline. Just annotate early November 2026 in your reporting (right alongside GSC’s other recent reporting changes) so you and your clients know why Search Console suddenly showed a vertical jump in clicks!

Disclaimer: This blog post was mostly generated by Gemini 4 Argon in the Antigravity harness in conjunction with Marie’s Brain – an OKF-driven system full of my knowledge. It has been fact-checked by me, Marie, a human (I think).

But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.)

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM

For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.)

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.)

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM

Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No."

We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM

While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

#7433. Engineering Manager, Automation Intelligence at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for companies that need to know who — or what — is on the other end of a request. Increasingly, the answer is not a person. AI agents, AI assistants, crawlers, headless browsers, and malicious automation now make up a large and fast-growing share of internet traffic, and telling them apart from humans — and from each other — is becoming one of the most important problems our customers ask us to solve.

We are standing up a dedicated Automation Intelligence engineering team to own that problem end to end: detection in the browser, detection at the edge, the classification taxonomy that tells customers what kind of automation they're seeing and how confident we are, and the API that customers and their agents call.

We're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead this team. You'll inherit a small, senior group (three engineers to start, growing to four or five) and a clear mandate. You report directly to the VP of Engineering.

This is a hands-on-adjacent engineering manager role for a small, senior, high-leverage team. You are not expected to write the production code — your engineers and their agents do that — but you are expected to be close enough to it to set direction, evaluate the work, and hold the quality bar.

The team has unusual autonomy and unusual visibility. It owns a product that leadership considers strategically critical, it is the first team operating Fingerprint's AI-native engineering model, and its results — good and bad — will be used as evidence for how the rest of engineering works. That means two things: you'll have real room to decide how the team operates, and you'll need to be honest about what the data shows.

In the first 90 days you will likely: finalize the roster and ownership lines with the sibling team, get the quality loop and engineering baselines running, deliver the engineering evidence for the Beta gate, and run the first review of the AI-native operating model.

At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team.  Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $159k - $215k

Alphabet’s Q3 numbers show AI Mode growing faster than it earns, and every reason Google gave for the slowdown is temporary except one.

Alphabet just reported the fastest growth in Google search queries in five years; in the same quarter, its search revenue grew at the slowest rate in 2026.

Roger covered the earnings call earlier this week on Search Engine Journal, and it’s a great overview of the high points. I’m diving deeper to make a specific point here.

Search & other revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion in the third quarter, according to Alphabet’s earnings release, down from 19% in the first quarter and 17% in the second. That was roughly $1.6 billion below analyst expectations, and CNBC reported it was the second straight quarter search came in under estimates. On the earnings call, Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, named one of the causes directly: strong growth in AI Mode queries “had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

For two years, the argument over whether AI answers cut into search has run on inferred numbers: click-through studies, panel estimates, and referral samples, many from vendors with something to sell. This quarter, the effect shows up in a counted number, Google’s own revenue line, with a Google executive naming AI Mode as a cause. That changes the quality of the evidence, even if it doesn’t finalize the argument.

A quick disclosure before going further: I run a company that measures visibility inside AI answers, so a story about money moving into those answers isn’t neutral ground for me.

The market reaction was severe. Alphabet shares fell about 13% on Thursday, the steepest one-day drop on record, erasing roughly half a trillion dollars in market value. Search wasn’t the only reason. Free cash flow came in at negative $9.07 billion against an expected shortfall of about $2.7 billion, and capital spending is still climbing. So I won’t claim investors sold because they rejected Google’s explanation for search. What I will claim is that the explanation needs a closer read than it’s getting, because the part that matters most is the part Google spent the least time on.

Schindler listed four drivers of the slowdown from the second quarter to the third. Foreign exchange came first, and he called it the single largest driver of the search revenue deceleration. Second, some retail advertisers in Asia-Pacific pulled back after the EU eliminated its de minimis exemption for low-value imports. Third, media and entertainment spending normalized after a second quarter inflated by the FIFA World Cup. Fourth, AI Mode queries grew quickly and earn less than traditional search. CFO Anat Ashkenazi added that Google has started lapping the search acceleration that began in the third quarter of 2025, which makes year-over-year comparisons harder for a few quarters.

Put those drivers on a timeline, and they sort themselves. A currency swing reverses or gets absorbed. The World Cup is over. A trade-rule change gets priced into advertiser budgets within a few quarters. Lapping a strong year is arithmetic that fades on its own. AI Mode is the only factor on the list that gets larger each quarter, because Google is actively growing it, and the lower monetization comes along with every query it adds.

Google’s Q3 explanation for slower search revenue named three temporary factors and one structural one: AI Mode queries are growing faster than they earn, and that gap widens with every quarter of adoption until ad yield inside the answer catches up.

I understand the instinct to dismiss the currency explanation as convenient. I’d rather check it, because Alphabet publishes enough to do that. Total revenue grew 25% in the third quarter whether or not you adjust for currency; the constant-currency reconciliation tables in the release show it, and Ashkenazi described FX as a slight headwind on year-over-year growth. In the second quarter, revenue grew 24%, or 23% in constant currency, which means currency added about a point. Across the whole company, then, currency moved from a slight tailwind to a slight headwind, a swing of a point or two at most.

Ashkenazi also said FX had a more significant impact on a sequential basis, and the release bears that out: Revenue grew 6% from the second quarter as reported and 7% in constant currency. That’s a real effect. It’s also a one-point effect, and it applies to the company as a whole, not to search specifically.

Search growth fell five points over the same period. Google doesn’t publish a constant-currency figure for search alone, so this can’t be determined precisely. But unless search is far more exposed to currency than the rest of Alphabet, my estimate is that FX accounts for something like one to two of those five points. That makes it plausible as the single largest driver, and it still leaves most of the slowdown to the other factors combined.

That distinction matters. “Single largest driver” is a ranking. It tells you FX beat each of the other causes individually. It doesn’t tell you FX explains most of the decline, and it says nothing about which causes will still be there next year. The currency explanation is probably true. It just isn’t the answer to the question investors and practitioners are actually asking, which is whether the new way people search with Google earns as much as the old one.

The other headline number deserves the same scrutiny. Sundar Pichai said Google’s year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it has been in five years. Google didn’t give the rate, and it didn’t say how a query is counted inside an AI Mode session. According to the call transcript, AI Mode queries average three times the length of traditional searches, and Google is now running multi-turn conversations in AI Mode, with ads designed for them. If each turn in a conversation counts as a query, query growth rises mechanically as conversations get longer, whether or not more people are searching for more things.

I’m not claiming that’s how Google counts. I’m saying the record query growth is a counted number with a definition we can’t see, and that kind of number should be held loosely until the definition is published. Revenue is much harder to redefine, which is why the revenue line is where the AI Mode story finally became visible.

In my forecast earlier in October that the SERP stops being Google’s default between 2028 and 2030, I argued the trigger is ad yield. Google flips the default when an answer earns roughly what a results page earns per query, because before that point flipping costs money and after it keeping the old default does. One of the signals I said would push the timeline later was weak returns from AI Mode ad placements.

Q3 is Google confirming, in its own revenue, that parity hasn’t arrived. That fits the forecast’s explanation for why Google isn’t in a hurry to flip anything. It also tells you where Google’s effort goes next. Google isn’t going to slow AI Mode down to protect the results page; Pichai credits AI for the query growth, and the company is plainly committed to it. Instead, Google closes the yield gap by putting more advertising inside the answer.

The call laid that plan out. Schindler said Google is scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries, taking AI Mode ads international for the first time, and introducing multi-turn ads in AI Mode in the U.S. He also said Google’s ad experiments have shown promising results, a phrase that will either become a reported metric in coming quarters or quietly disappear.

None of this surprised me. In August 2025, I described an ad system that builds the ad at query time inside the response, with advertisers supplying inputs rather than finished creative, and placement decided by how closely a brand aligns with the intent behind the prompt. Google shipped an early version at Google Marketing Live in May. Q3 explains why the rest of that design is likely to arrive faster: Google now has a quarterly revenue reason to finish building it.

One line from the call should get more attention from SEOs than it will. Schindler said click-through rates “are already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode.” On a traditional results page, organic and paid listings occupied different territory with different click behavior, and practitioners built entire strategies around that separation. Inside an AI Mode answer, by Google’s own account, a sponsored product listing and an organic one draw clicks at about the same rate.

Put that next to the yield gap and my read is straightforward, though I want to be clear it’s my opinion and not something Google said. An answer has a small number of places where a brand can appear. As Google adds ads to close the gap, more of those places become available for purchase, and if sponsored and organic placements perform alike, advertisers have every reason to buy them. Organic visibility inside the answer doesn’t disappear, but it now competes for space with inventory that carries a direct revenue target.

Google also said the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, and that many are upper-funnel queries carrying new commercial intent. That’s Google’s claim, and nobody outside Google can verify it. If it’s accurate, AI Mode is creating commercial moments that never existed on the results page, and the decision about which brands appear in them happens inside the answer, before anyone clicks anything. That’s a strong argument for measuring presence in the answer and not just clicks out of it.

The practical move is to establish a baseline now, before ad load inside AI Mode scales. For the queries that matter most in your category, record which answers cite you, which cite competitors, and which already carry sponsored units alongside the citations. A quarter from now, that record tells you whether paid placements are taking positions organic sources used to hold, and it gives you evidence to bring to budget conversations instead of an impression. Google will report its side of this story in aggregate. Nobody is going to report yours for you.

This is where the difference between counted and inferred numbers stops being academic. Google’s revenue line is counted and audited. The query growth claim is counted but undefined. The incremental-query claim is asserted. Click-through studies of AI answers are inferred from samples. Each deserves a different level of trust, and the mistake I see most often is treating them as interchangeable because they all arrive as percentages. Measuring how brands actually show up inside AI answers, rather than inferring it from traffic, is the problem I built CitationIQ to address, and it becomes harder and more necessary as paid placements fill those answers.

Google’s fourth-quarter report arrives in early February, and Ashkenazi has already said FX will be a slightly larger headwind and lapping will cost a couple of points of growth. Q4 comes with the same cover built in. Here’s what I’ll be looking at instead:

The third-quarter report is the first time the gap between how much people use Google’s AI search and how much it earns appeared in Google’s own revenue, and Google’s response to that gap will be more advertising inside AI answers, where paid and organic placements now compete for the same small set of positions.

#7429. With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent.

I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

Tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. Tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

For one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

Redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

@MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

Creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

#7427. Senior Manager, Application Security at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

As Fingerprint scales with large enterprise customers in financial services and fraud prevention, we're investing in application security as a dedicated, first-class discipline. We're looking for a Senior Manager, Application Security to lead that investment, reporting directly to the VP of Engineering. You will personally own and build the AppSec program, and you will also manage a small team of experienced practitioners who run IT operations and compliance.

This is a VP-direct role with high autonomy and high visibility. Enterprise customers regularly ask about Fingerprint's security posture. You'll be the person who owns that answer.

Cross-functional Leadership & Communication

This role is AppSec-first with a management scope that spans IT and compliance. That shape is deliberate. Application security is where we're investing next, and we want someone who can personally build it — not just oversee it. At the same time, IT and compliance are already run by experienced practitioners who don't need a domain expert over them; they need a leader who gives them direction, context, and prioritization.

What this means in practice: you will be hands-on in AppSec and hands-off-but-accountable in IT and compliance. We don't expect you to arrive as an expert in IT operations or GRC. We do expect you to learn those domains quickly — well enough within your first few months to evaluate your team's work, make prioritization calls across all three disciplines, and represent each of them credibly to leadership and customers. The judgment to know when to rely on your team vs. when to drive the decision yourself is what distinguishes the right candidate.

This is a role for someone who is still a strong practitioner in AppSec and has grown into leading people — not for someone who has moved entirely out of technical work, and not for a pure individual contributor who hasn't managed before.

At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team.  Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $177k - $240kSome example salaries for specific locations are below:

Final offer amounts are determined by multiple factors, including the successful candidate's location, experience, and expertise, and may vary from the amounts listed above.

Due to regulatory and security reasons, there’s a small number of countries where we cannot have Fingerprint teammates based. Additionally, because Fingerprint is an all-remote company and people can join our workforce from almost any country, we do not sponsor visas. Fingerprint teammates need to be authorized to work from their home location.

We are dedicated to creating an inclusive work environment for everyone. We embrace and celebrate the unique experiences, perspectives and cultural backgrounds that each employee brings to our workplace. Fingerprint strives to foster an environment where our employees feel respected, valued and empowered, and our team members are at the forefront in helping us promote and sustain an inclusive workplace. We highly encourage people from underrepresented groups in tech to apply.

If you are applying as a resident of California, please read our CCPA notice here.

If you are applying as a resident of the EU, please read our GDPR notice here.

**We have noticed a rise in recruiting impersonations across the industry, where scammers attempt to access candidates' personal and financial information through fake interviews and offers. All Fingerprint recruiting email communications will always come from the @fingerprint.com domain. Any outreach claiming to be from Fingerprint via other sources should be ignored.

#7425. Meta pulls down controversial terms of service

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”

Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

The FTC unsealed new details in its Amazon Ads lawsuit, alleging hidden surcharges raised CPCs by up to 250% on Prime Day. Here is what advertisers should know.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 22 state attorneys general filed an updated complaint against Amazon with newly unredacted details about how the company allegedly inflated prices in its online search advertising auction.

The FTC and its state partners originally sued Amazon in August in the Western District of Washington, alleging the retailer covertly raised the prices advertisers paid on its platforms.

The newly unsealed material alleges that Amazon secretly increased advertising prices by up to 50% above auction results on ordinary days. During major shopping events like Prime Day and Black Friday, the alleged increases reached 250%.

Read on to learn what the unredacted complaint alleges, how Amazon responded to advertiser questions at the time, and what this means for how you evaluate historical campaign performance.

According to the FTC’s November 5 announcement, the unsealed sections of the complaint outline specific cost-per-click (CPC) increases and revenue targets tied to the alleged surcharges between 2021 and 2023.

The complaint alleges that Amazon’s hidden surcharges affected both small businesses and large advertisers across multiple peak shopping periods:

These examples add detail to the original lawsuit, which challenged how Amazon calculated auction prices and explained those calculations to advertisers.

The unsealed material also links Amazon’s alleged surcharges to internal revenue goals.

According to the complaint, Amazon executives discussed needing an additional $40 million in revenue in 2023 to hit corporate financial targets.

The complaint quotes an email from the head of Amazon Ads to Amazon’s senior vice president of ad products and technology:

I’d like to pull out all of the stops (without doing unnatural acts) to close our gaps to plan. I suspect that the entire gap won’t be closed, so whatever can be done with reserves (ideally at least $40MM would be helpful).

The case concerns Amazon’s use of “soft reserve prices,” which can increase the final CPC above what competing bids would otherwise produce.

A soft reserve differs from a minimum bid required to enter an auction. Amazon says advertisers can win placements below the soft reserve, in which case they pay their bid.

The FTC alleges Amazon used undisclosed reserve pricing to increase advertiser charges while continuing to describe its auctions in misleading terms.

If you managed Amazon Ads between 2021 and 2023, you may remember questioning why CPCs jumped so sharply during peak shopping events.

According to the unredacted complaint, advertisers questioned Amazon directly about whether changes to its auction process explained higher CPCs.

In one instance, an advertiser asked whether “something has changed with respect to the second price auction process, either by design or mistake.”

The FTC alleges that an Amazon account manager gave a misleading response:

After reaching out to the product specialist team we were informed there is not a bug, or a change in auction style, so no worries there. This year the marketplace is even more crowded than any year previous, and we are seeing the spike in CPCs [costs-per-click] as a direct reflection.

The alleged exchange concerns more than whether CPCs increased. It concerns whether Amazon accurately explained the cause when an advertiser asked about changes to the auction.

Campaign reports show what advertisers paid and the performance that followed. They do not reveal how Amazon calculated the final CPC.

In its response to the original lawsuit, Amazon denied deceiving or harming advertisers. The company defended its reserve pricing and said advertisers never pay more than their maximum bid.

While these allegations are still being litigated in federal court, the unsealed details give paid media teams important context for past and current campaign analysis.

If you manage Amazon Ads for your brand or clients, here’s a few proactive steps you can take:

The 2021 through 2023 examples also shouldn’t be read as the full scope of the case. Earlier FTC materials discuss alleged conduct in 2024 and identify Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, and Display Ads.

The FTC’s press release summarizes the newly unredacted allegations, but it doesn’t state whether the alleged surcharge practices continued past 2023 or which specific Amazon search ad formats were included.

The newest release didn’t include a public response from Amazon regarding the newly unsealed details, however, Amazon did provide a full response dispute on August 31st regarding the lawsuit.

We’ll continue to report on this as more information from the court filings becomes available, or if Amazon provides an updated response to this new information.

Salon, one of the first digital-native news outlets, closed this week after 31 years. Which one of these journalists did not work at Salon at some point?

“Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier,” the site wrote anonymously at its passing. Its last owner describes its core business as “Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto.”

The Needle scarred a generation of politics junkies with its constant jittering — and by giving Hillary Clinton an 82% chance of victory well into 2016’s election night.
